newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: World business group urges global investment pact.
newsitem.headline: World business group urges global investment pact.

text.p: The main world business organisation, the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC), on Thursday urged developed and developing countries to work quickly for a global agreement on investment rules.

The call was issued at the start of a one-day Forum on Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) organised by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) which has attracted government and business leaders from many states.

"No single country in the world has the capacity to develop all the goods, services, capital and technology that its citizens need and demand," ICC official Douglas Gregory of Canada told the Forum in a keynote address.
"As a result, all countries must rely on trade and investment from other countries in order to meet the demands of the local market."

But while a large body of international trade law had developed -- under the old General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) and in the new World Trade Organisation (WTO) -- there was no similar structure for investment.
"This has made the need for a coherent multilateral framework of rules on investment all the more pressing," declared Gregory, a senior advisor on trade and investment to IBM Canada Ltd.

The Forum was called to discuss UNCTAD's World Investment Report last month which found FDI was running at a record level of $315 billion in 1995 as transnational corporations (TNCs) move rapidly to build up global business structures.

But UNCTAD's declared aim was also to help governments prepare, through debate of the often controversial issues involved, for the WTO's first ministerial conference in December in Singapore, where major powers want investment on the agenda.

The Secretary-General of UNCTAD, former Brazilian finance minister Rubens Ricupero, told the Forum it was vital to "integrate the different approaches" that existed towards FDI among government, the private sector and labour bodies.

Many emerging economies, including India and Malaysia, oppose even study of whether investment rules are needed in the WTO -- fearing this would inevitably put pressure on them to treat foreign investors as favourably as local business.
This, they argue, would allow powerful TNC's to squeeze out fledgling local firms and then establish control not only over prices but over entire national economies.

Gregory, whose ICC includes firms from all business sectors around the globe, made clear that what the ICC wanted was a WTO accord that would enshrine the principle of "national treatment" -- or full equality for local and outside investors.

He said an accord should provide protection for FDI, remove current barriers to investment in many countries, and establish a mechanism for dispute resolution -- on the lines of the WTO's new dispute procedure covering goods and services.
WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero told an UNCTAD meeting on Tuesday that a report his organisation is issuing next week would make a "compelling case" for bringing FDI under its wing.

Speakers at the Forum from developing countries, including Bangladesh and Ethiopia, said they recognised that attitudes to FDI in emerging countries had changed and that it was now seen as a motor for growth rather than a threat.

But Madagascar's Minister of Industry and External Trade Alain Ramaroson said his country still wanted to be able to choose what outside investment was needed and to which sectors of the economy it should be guided.

And papers distributed by non-governmental organisations from Asia argued that opening wide borders to investment -- even under WTO rules -- would imperil sovereignty and the right to determine what economic policies were best for a nation.
